w: Founded in 1818 by King Joao VI as the 'Royal Museum,' this became Brazil's oldest scientific institution, housed in a former royal and imperial palace. On 2 September 2018 a faulty air conditioner sparked a fire that nearby hydrants couldn't fight -- some 92% of its 20-million-item collection burned in a single night.
s: Brazil's oldest museum, gutted by fire in one night
_facts: Founded 1818 by King Joao VI as the 'Royal Museum'
Oldest scientific institution in Brazil
Housed in the former Braganza royal/imperial palace
2018 fire destroyed roughly 92% of its 20 million items

w: The seat of the Archdiocese of Rio de Janeiro, dedicated to Saint Sebastian -- the city's own patron saint. Every Archbishop of Rio has held their cathedra here, the literal seat of the office the cathedral is named for.
s: Rio's cathedral, named for the city's patron saint
_facts: Seat of the Archdiocese of Rio de Janeiro
Dedicated to Saint Sebastian, patron saint of Rio

w: Now one of Rio's most affluent addresses, wedged between the Lagoa and the beach, Leblon began life as a quilombo -- a settlement of escaped slaves, established by a Portuguese abolitionist landowner. Little of that history shows on the surface today; it's better known now for the beach that shares its name.
s: An escaped-slave settlement, now Rio's poshest beach
_facts: Began as a quilombo of escaped slaves
Founded by a Portuguese abolitionist landowner
Now a very affluent South Zone neighbourhood

w: Thirteen kilometres of box girder strung across Guanabara Bay, connecting Rio to Niteroi since 1974 -- for over a decade it was the second-longest bridge on Earth. Its central span rises 72 metres above the water, just enough clearance for ships. More than 150,000 vehicles a day still cross it.
s: A record-breaking bridge across Guanabara Bay
_facts: Completed 1974, connecting Rio and Niteroi
World's second-longest bridge from 1974-1985
Central span 72m high, 300m long
Carries over 150,000 vehicles daily

w: Portuguese sailors named this granite monolith for the shape of a ship's topsail when they sighted it on New Year's Day, 1502. Weathering has carved what looks like a giant human face into one side, and marks on another have been read as an ancient inscription. Geologists say it's just erosion and pareidolia.
s: A mountain with a face carved by weather, not hands
_facts: Named 'Rock of the Topsail' by sailors who sighted it 1 Jan 1502
Differential weathering created a face-like formation
Geologists attribute the 'face' and 'inscription' to erosion and pareidolia
One of the highest mountains ending directly in the ocean

w: Every tree in this forest is a replant. Coffee farms had stripped the hillsides bare and threatened the capital's drinking water, so during the Second Empire the whole mountain was deliberately reforested from scratch. Capuchin monkeys, coatis, agoutis and marmosets now treat it as home.
s: A rainforest that was deliberately replanted from scratch
_facts: Entirely secondary vegetation, reforested during the Second Empire
Reforestation was a response to coffee-farm deforestation threatening water supply
Over 230 animal and bird species now live there

w: Oscar Niemeyer's flying saucer, dropped onto a cliff above Boa Viagem beach in 1996 -- a 16-metre cupola ringed by an 817-square-metre reflecting pool he described as a flower. It holds over 1,200 works from collector Joao Sattamini's trove, the second-largest contemporary art collection in Brazil.
s: Niemeyer's UFO-shaped museum on a cliff
_facts: Designed by Oscar Niemeyer, completed 1996
Collection of 1,217 works from Joao Sattamini
Structure likened to a UFO; featured landing in a Niemeyer documentary

w: Built purely so samba schools could parade competitively, this is where Rio Carnival's real contest happens every year, watched by thousands packed along Oscar Niemeyer's purpose-built passarela. It was Niemeyer's first major commission after Brazil's military dictatorship ended in 1985.
s: Where Carnival's samba schools go to compete
_facts: Purpose-built for Rio Carnival's competitive samba parades
Designed by Oscar Niemeyer
His first major work after the 1964-1985 dictatorship ended

w: Machado de Assis declared this academy founded on 15 December 1896, and it's run on the same logic since: forty members, called 'the immortals,' elected for life from Brazil's most accomplished writers. No law gives it authority, yet its dictionary of correct Portuguese is treated as final.
s: Forty 'immortals' who decide what counts as a word
_facts: Founded 15 December 1896 by first president Machado de Assis
40 lifetime members known as 'the immortals'
Its Orthographic Vocabulary is the de facto authority on Brazilian Portuguese

w: Since the early 1950s, Lapa has been where Rio's musicians, artists and intellectuals actually go -- a tight grid of bars and venues built around the colonial-era Passeio Publico, the city's first public park, laid out in 1783. It runs the gamut from street samba to Sala Cecilia Meireles' chamber music.
_facts: Known for lively nightlife and Brazilian music since the early 1950s
Home to the Passeio Publico, Rio's first public park (1783)
Sala Cecilia Meireles chamber music venue is here

w: A church built in stages across more than a century, from 1775 into the late 1800s -- long enough that its Portuguese colonial Baroque facade doesn't match what's inside, where Neoclassical and Neo-Renaissance work took over as tastes changed. One building, several centuries of fashion.
s: One church facade, a century of changing tastes inside
_facts: Built and decorated from 1775 to the late 19th century
Portuguese colonial Baroque facade
Neoclassical and Neo-Renaissance interior elements

w: The largest urban seaside park on Earth, stretched along Guanabara Bay to fill the gap between downtown Rio and Copacabana. Most people just call it the Aterro; its full official name, Eduardo Gomes Park, rarely gets used at all.
s: The biggest urban seaside park on the planet
_facts: Largest urban seaside park in the world
Also known as Aterro do Flamengo / Eduardo Gomes Park
Runs along Guanabara Bay between Downtown Rio and Copacabana

w: The rack railway that hauls visitors up from Cosme Velho to the 710-metre summit of Corcovado, where the line ends practically at the feet of Christ the Redeemer. Same steep climb, same view over the city and its beaches, that's been drawing people up this mountain for generations.
s: The train that climbs to Christ the Redeemer
_facts: Mountain rack railway from Cosme Velho to Corcovado's summit
Summit is 710 metres, site of Christ the Redeemer

w: Named for a small church built in the early 1900s by Conrado Jacob Niemeyer, this pocket of the South Zone has one of Brazil's highest standards of living -- right against the border of Rocinha, one of the country's largest favelas. It's known for hang gliding, and for Casa das Canoas, Oscar Niemeyer's own modernist house.
s: Wealth, hang gliders and a favela, all next door
_facts: Named after a church built by Conrado Jacob Niemeyer, early 20th c.
Borders Rocinha, one of Brazil's largest favelas
Casa das Canoas, Oscar Niemeyer's own house, is here
